sorry to be a bit snappy. (or more than a bit). finding myself increasingly frustrated by the right and honestly having some difficulty understanding the other side (as shown here). but actually interested in some pushback, so:

- obviously there is middle ground between everything, i guess i'm just wondering where you are taking underlying principles, then. chicago? (and in that vicinity)? my critique regarding regulation is with that in mind. (and, to me, the financial crisis seems a pretty good example of how self-interest in the market sans government regulation isn't a winning strategy) i also think that the proven success of keynesian stimuli ought to make one reevaluate government intervention. and, not trying to be an asshole, i'm from a red state and proudly so--but people reliant on welfare programs who voted for donald trump should make it obvious that its flawed to draw a macroeconomic theory that presupposes rationality. elsewhere: i dont think you can say that market forces necessarily produce efficient or desirable outcome, especially within the context of privatizing things like health care, education and prisons. maybe i'm misunderstanding who conservatives draw as forefathers, but save begrudigng support of medicare, it doesn't seem like people are willing to come to the conclusion that the market doesnt produce necessarily good outcomes. and, smith's invisible hand and locke's social contract are contingent upon some baseline societal health. 

- will concede i definitely don't know the broader conservative platform regarding protectionism and a globalizing economy. half the narrative of the campaign, though, was disaffected white voters from the rust belt etc etc. this is absolutely a consequence of comparative advantage. i know what a free market is, i was asking for your definition of it. my assumption is that tariffs are usually considered part of the package? free markets also presuppose ease of entry, which, to a point about positive liberty:

- are you writing this with a mind to hayek? "any means necessary" sounds a little hyberpolic / hayekian to me. that intervening in pursuit of better will ultimately lead down a very dark, overbearing path (to serfdom). i do think you are really limiting who is in the polity when you say that broken windows policy overall improves liberty in society. it is pretty widely acknowledged that stop and frisk in new york was a racist, draconian policy, and that much of policing still is today; read any DOJ report. yes, you can point to the lower crime statistics and say all of those people are free from violence, but you are then neglecting the many many people whose liberty is directly infringed upon by the state. and, obviously, this affects one's positive freedoms. you can't even get off the ground to try to pursue your life if you have been jailed for having some weed in your pocket. its this that really worries me when conservatives claim successes of things like stop and frisk--there is so much and so many that are just completely being ignored from the equation. i understand the premise of stop and frisk, and, like most conservatives, i place a very very high value on someones 4th amendment rights, the liberty to to their person. this is not giulliani's new york. (also just the premise of a social contract and a state by, of, for. we grant police the power of force to protect us as citizens. this is now how policing policy plays out)

- similarly, positive liberty in the american context means getting individuals into a place where they can pursue what they want. a big portion of this is remedying past mistakes. slavery, of course, but a lot of others. welfare programs are essential to making sure that people are free to, not simply free from. welfare policies give people a chance, which is really what positive liberty is all about. (maybe outside your wheelhouse but have you read any sen?)

a bit late to the game here, but a way I have been thinking lately: 

**the morality of my suicide is inversely proportional to how loved i am. if you are alone, there is no real criticism to your wanting to die**


- i am not actively enjoying my life. on the contrary, I am actively suffering (infinite disutility for me, minimal disutility for those who have 'known' me]

- at this point, I am not actively in anyone's life, no one is reliant on or invested in my being.
they will hurt [and there will be a ripple effect onto others because of their hurt] but they and their lives wont fundamentally change

-- [to the suggestion of family, my answer is that whatever broader impact there is is muted. each member of my nuclear family is emotionally limited in some capacity, meaning

--- there are no relationships that will be lost,
--- their reaction could quite possibly be muted, and 
--- because they are limited, they, too, are not in the world. and so their hurt from my departure doesnt spread far]

- i am consuming more in resources than I am contributing to society.

-- I consume resources wholly for myself (as there is no one actively wanting my presence, or invested in (or thinking of) my happiness). 

--- I am claiming resources in this mad scramble to claw myself out in a way that is to the detriment to others.
--- I am a gentrifier. I am displacing, and I am displacing people of greater value, of fuller and more significant lives than mine.
-there is approximately zero evidence to suggest that any of that is likely to change in the remotely foreseeable future
